An interloper is a person who enters a place, situation, group, or activity where they are not wanted and where others feel they have no right to be.

Three things work together to make someone an interloper. First, they have pushed themselves into some kind of "space" — this could be a physical place, a social circle, a professional field, a private conversation, or a relationship. Second, they were not invited. Third, and most importantly, the people who were already there strongly feel that this person does not belong and has no business being there.

Think of it this way: imagine a tight group of old friends who meet every Friday night. One day, someone none of them know well starts showing up uninvited, sitting down, joining conversations, and acting like they belong. To that group of friends, this person is an interloper — an unwelcome presence who has inserted themselves into a space that wasn't theirs to enter.
The Key Idea Hidden Inside the Word

The most important thing to understand about "interloper" is that it always reflects a point of view. It is a label that the people already in a space put on the newcomer. It says: "You don't belong here. We didn't ask for you. This is not your place."

This means the person being called an interloper may not actually be doing anything wrong in an absolute sense. They might even have a legitimate reason to be there. But the word expresses how others feel about their presence — unwelcome, resentful, and protective of their space.
What Makes This Word Different From Similar Words

It helps to understand "interloper" by seeing how it differs from words that seem close to it.

An intruder usually breaks into a physical space, often forcefully or illegally — like someone who enters your home without permission. The emphasis is on the physical act of breaking in.

An outsider is simply someone who is not part of a group. It is neutral and descriptive. It carries no judgment.

A trespasser specifically enters property they have no legal right to be on.

An interloper is broader and more flexible than all of these. It does not have to involve physical space at all, and it does not have to involve anything illegal. It is about social and situational belonging. Someone can be an interloper in a business deal, in a conversation, in a romantic situation, in a professional field, in a neighborhood circle, or in a country's politics. The sting of the word is not about law — it is about the feeling of "you simply do not belong here, and you have had the nerve to show up anyway."
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Interloper" carries a distinctly negative and somewhat indignant tone. When someone uses this word, they are not being neutral — they are expressing frustration, resentment, or disapproval toward the person who has entered uninvited. It is the verbal equivalent of crossed arms.

The word also carries a subtle suggestion that the interloper is self-serving — that they are in this space to gain something (power, access, profit, attention) that they have not earned the right to pursue there.

It is not a casual or mild word. Calling someone an interloper is a fairly sharp accusation that they are overstepping.
The Many Situations Where This Word Applies

One of the most useful things about "interloper" is how widely it applies across different situations.

In social life: A person who constantly inserts themselves into a close friendship, trying to become part of something they were never part of, can be called an interloper by those friends.

In business and professional life: If a company from outside an industry suddenly starts competing in a market that established players feel is "theirs," those existing players might refer to the newcomer as an interloper — an outsider with no history or earned place in their field.

In relationships: If a third person interferes in a romantic relationship or close friendship, they can be described as an interloper — someone who has no right to be in that intimate space between two people.

In politics and international affairs: When a foreign government, organization, or power gets involved in the affairs of another country or community without being asked, those on the receiving end may call them interlopers — unwelcome forces meddling where they do not belong.

In physical spaces: Someone who wanders into a private gathering, a restricted area, or a community they have no connection to can be an interloper in the eyes of those who feel ownership over that space.
An Important Nuance: It Does Not Mean "Wrong"

This is subtle but important. Being labeled an interloper does not automatically mean the person is morally wrong or acting badly. It only means that the people who were already there view them as unwelcome. History is full of examples where people were called interlopers simply for entering spaces others wanted to keep exclusive — and they had every right to be there.

So when you encounter this word, always ask: Who is calling this person an interloper, and why do they feel that way? The word tells you a great deal about the feelings of the people using it, and sometimes less about whether the so-called interloper is actually in the wrong.

An interloper is an uninvited, unwelcome person who has pushed into a place, group, situation, or activity where others strongly feel they have no right to be. The word is judgmental in tone, reflects the perspective of those who feel their space has been invaded, and can apply to physical, social, professional, or political situations. Its core emotional charge is: you do not belong here, and yet here you are.
